# Imagined vs. Actual “Others” An Experiment on Interethnic Giving in Afghanistan

∞

Luke N. Condra

∗ Mohammad Isaqzadeh

† Sera Linardi

‡ This version: July 27, 2016

Abstract Does willingness to aid “others” change when in their physical presence? We argue that studies cueing non-coethnics through names and photos may underestimate discrimination resulting from actual interethnic interaction. In an experiment in Kabul, Afghanistan, Dari-speaking day-laborers contribute their earnings to a hospital under one of three randomly-assigned experimental conditions. In In-group, the hospital is in a Dari-speaking province; in Out-group-Abstract and Out-group-Real, it is in a Pashto-speaking (Pashtun) province. While subjects in In-group and Outgroup-Abstract wait for the experiment with only Dari-speakers present, subjects in Out-group-Real wait among both Dari-speakers and Pashto-speakers. When Pashtuns are absent, the findings accord with other experiments that find little to no out-group discrimination. However, the physical presence of Pashtuns (Out-group-Real) decreases contributions by 25%. Consistent with the threat hypothesis, contributions decrease the longer Dari-speakers wait with Pashtuns, though subjects’ youth and ability to speak Pashto mediate this effect.

1

Is there taste-based discrimination against ethnic-out groups? The empirical literature examining

this question has returned mixed results. On the one hand, experiments that cue the out-group in

lab-style economic games in an ‘abstract’ way to subjects through photographs (e.g., Habyarimana

et al. 2007), ethnically identifiable names (e.g., Fershtman and Gneezy 2001), or outright

disclosure of ethnic identity (e.g., Chuah et al. 2014) find little to no evidence of discrimination

toward the out-group. But experiments that physically expose subjects to the out-group find much

stronger evidence of discriminatory behavior or prejudicial attitudes resulting from interaction (e.g.,

Adida, Laitin, and Valfort forthcoming, Enos 2014). What accounts for this discrepancy? Are

there important triggers of ethnic identity that are present in the flesh but not in the abstract?

To address this question, we conducted a field experiment in which we raise contributions for

a real public good (a hospital), among day laborers in Kabul, Afghanistan. In the experiment we

employ an abstract cue of ethnic identity separately from a real cue of the out-group via physical

exposure to compare the effects of each. We take advantage of the relatively clean ethno-linguistic

cleavage in society where the Pashtuns, who remained politically dominant after the bloody

interethnic Afghan civil war of the 1990s,

1 speak Pashto as their first language while most non-

Pashtun minorities speak Dari. We focus on whether Dari-speakers give (anonymously) less to a

hospital in the Pashto-speaking Helmand province (Out-group treatment) than they do to the

branch in the Dari-speaking Panjshir province (In-group treatment). We manipulated the salience

of ethnic cues in the Out-group treatment by having the Dari-speaker wait for the experiment

amongst only other Dari speakers (Abstract) or also with some Pashto speakers present (Real).

1 Between 1992 and 2000, scholars estimate at least 27,500 battle deaths in this civil war (Lacina

and Gleditsch 2005).


<!-- Page 3 -->


2

The nature of the physical interaction is not determined by the experimenters, but left entirely to

the discretion and choice of the subjects, as it would be in real life.

We find that subjects do not discriminate against out-group Pashtuns when out-group members

are not present (Out-group-Abstract). But discrimination is significant when Pashtuns are physically

present (Out-group-Real). The decrease in contributions is stark – about 25% – and shows that an

absence of discrimination against the out-group in the abstract does not equate to no

discrimination in the flesh.

To explore possible mechanisms driving this behavior, we make use of the fact that the length

of time that subjects were physically exposed to the Pashtun out-group before the contribution

decision is exogenously determined because subjects were called in random order to be

enumerated. We find that contributions decrease the longer subjects waited alongside the Pashto-

speakers. This suggests that due to Pashtuns’ historical dominance in Afghanistan, the perception

of threat, or the salience of ethnic identity, increased for the Dari-speakers as the time of exposure

to spoken Pashto increased. If that is the case, then an observable implication is that those subjects

whose personal characteristics would increase the perceived threat from hearing Pashto – namely

those who are not bilingual in Pashto and those who were born before the carnage of the 1990s

civil war – should be more negatively affected by spoken Pashto. Indeed, we find this to be true.

Our contributions are several. First, our study shows that finding no discrimination in response

to an abstract cue of the out-group does not mean there will not be discrimination when the out-

group is physically present. Our experimental design enables us to establish this finding in an

environment where the existence and length of physical exposure is randomly assigned, avoiding

the problem in observational studies where subjects may have selected to live or remain in places

where they are physically exposed to the out-group.


<!-- Page 4 -->


3

Second, several features of our experiment contribute to the external validity of our results.

While lab experiments have contributed greatly to our theories of intergroup contact, it can be

difficult to generalize their findings to complex and volatile environments such as the one we study

here. Subjects are drawn from the same population – low income Afghans – whose behavior we

care about understanding. We embed the experiment in the context of a real and relevant

charitable organization, so far from playing a ‘game’, subjects are confronted with an opportunity to

contribute to a public good.

2 Moreover, the treatment is naturalistic. Subjects are left to wait with

others, as they would while waiting to vote or to receive services. This emulates situations where

strangers mix together for a random period of time, and in which power dynamics that are missing

in lab interactions emerge and may affect behavior.

Third, our results contribute to an emerging and interesting set of results on how duration of

exposure to the out-group affects attitudes and behavior toward the out-group in everyday life. We

show that increasing duration of physical exposure to the out-group – which ranges from a few

minutes to about five hours – negatively affects altruism toward the out-group. Very few studies

have examined this question,

3 but putting our results together with the few that have suggests an

2 Charitable giving is a normal and familiar activity in Islam  (Lambarraa and Riener 2012).

3 For example, Enos (2014) finds a statistically significant increase in discriminatory attitudes

towards Mexicans among whites after three consecutive days of brief physical exposure (<30

minutes) to Mexicans; however, this increase is no longer significant after ten consecutive days of

exposure. Alexander and Christia (2011) finds that students who attended an ethnically segregated

school gave less in a public goods game if the players are multi-ethnic. This is not true of students

from ethnically mixed schools.


<!-- Page 5 -->


4

inverse-U-shaped relationship: discrimination initially increases with physical exposure to the out-

group but then decreases when exposure is repeated over the long term (e.g., weeks).

Fourth, we speculate on the nature of factors that might mediate these negative effects of out-

group exposure through analysis of heterogeneous treatment effects in our sample. Our reasoning

here is post hoc and thus should be considered exploratory, but makes an important point that

should be tested in future research. We find that physical exposure to the out-group does not

cause discrimination among young and bilingual subjects. We reason that language acts as a vehicle

for integration or a sign that someone already has integrated with the out-group, enabling higher

quality interaction. Similarly, relative youth may represent little to no memory of the civil war of

the 1990s that was fought largely along ethnic lines. While such factors are context-dependent,

these findings suggest that the process of integration will differ depending on personal

characteristics that enable meaningful interethnic communication and decrease the impact of

historical antagonisms between groups.

Theoretical Motivation

Many observational studies on the effect of ethnic diversity on attitudes and behavior toward the

out-group find evidence in favor of the contact hypothesis,

4 but these results may suffer from

selection problems, whereby prejudiced people might avoid intergroup contact, biasing results

(Hopkins 2010, 49, Pettigrew 1998). As such, scholars have turned to lab and field experiments to

4 The evidence is particularly strong when certain conditions from Allport (1954) are present: equal

status between the groups in the situation; common goals exit for groups; the situation encourages

intergroup cooperation; and authorities, law, or custom support the interaction (Pettigrew and

Tropp 2006).


<!-- Page 6 -->


5

isolate the independent effect of ethnic mixing on prosocial behavior (usually in standard

economic games), exposing subjects to the out-group. We review this literature in terms of the kind

of cue provided, in the ‘abstract’ and through ‘real’ physical exposure.

Subjects have been exposed to the out-group in the ‘abstract’ in three main ways. One is

through the use of photographs that reveal others’ race to subjects (e.g., Burns 2004, Fong and

Luttmer 2009, Habyarimana et al. 2007). Though the geographic settings of these experiments

differ widely, the consistent finding is that partner’s race does not affect the size of offers in these

dictator-style games, or even attitudes toward the out-group (Havekes, Coenders, and Van der

Lippe 2013). Similarly, experiments that have used names commonly associated with a particular

ethnic or religious group to ‘abstractly’ cue trust/dictator game partner’s ethnic identity have found

no significant differences in average offers made to the out-group (Bouckaert and Dhaene 2004,

Chuah, Fahoum, and Hoffmann 2013, Fershtman and Gneezy 2001). This is also the case when

ethnic identity is cued by simply stating or revealing a game partner’s ethnicity outright (e.g., Chuah

et al. 2014, Waring and Bell 2013).

In contrast, studies with real (rather than abstract) exposure to the out-group suggest that there

indeed is discrimination toward the out-group. For example, Enos (2014) finds an increase in anti-

Mexican attitudes in surveys when white commuters waited alongside Mexicans for trains, while

Alexander and Christia (2011) find smaller contributions in public goods games with abstract out-

group ethnic cues among students who attended an ethnically segregated school.

However, various design features in these studies make it difficult to compare the effect of

abstract vs. real exposure on behavior. For example, some studies feature physical exposure to the

out-group, but not an abstract cue (e.g., Enos 2014), while others feature an abstract cue but not a

real cue of ethnic identity within the experiment itself (e.g., Alexander and Christia 2011). Others


<!-- Page 7 -->


6

investigate how physical exposure affects attitudes, but not behavior (Enos 2014). Still others focus

on third party sanctioning as a mechanism for inducing prosocial behavior across ethnic lines (e.g.,

Bernhard, Fischbacher, and Fehr 2006, Jeon, Johnson, and Robinson forthcoming), an

institutional addition that we do not pursue here due to our focus on pure taste-based

discrimination.

Even for studies that are most similar to ours in their design, abstract and real cues are both

included, making it difficult to separate their effects on contributions to the public good. For

example, though coethnics trust each other more than non-coethnics while playing trust games

together in Malawian market areas (real cue), the partner’s ethnic identity is communicated by

revealing her ethnically-homogenous home village (abstract cue), so the effects of the two cue types

are not investigated separately (Robinson forthcoming). Similarly, increasing the number of

Senegalese Muslims in a dictator game session decreases French donors’ offers to Senegalese

Muslim partners (real cue), but session diversity is communicated through the number of Muslim

names revealed on a screen (abstract cue) (Adida, Laitin, and Valfort forthcoming). In contrast, we

want to isolate the effects of abstract and real cueing of the out-group in the same experiment in

order to test whether there is a difference in how they affect behavior.

These literatures on the effects of abstract and real cues of the out-group on prosocial behavior

have developed largely in parallel to each other. Our synthesis of these two literatures suggests that

behavior toward the out-group is affected differently by abstract and real cues of the out-group. To

investigate this question, we must first include both types of exposure to the out-group in the same

experiment but also be able to estimate their effects separately. Second, we should test an

argument in the literature, whether physical exposure increases out-group discrimination by


<!-- Page 8 -->


7

randomly varying the length of physical exposure to the out-group,

5 providing a continuous

measure of physical exposure as a proxy for the salience of ethnic identity. This should provide an

exogenous increase in the salience of ethnic identity among those who had physical exposure to

the out-group. We should expect more discrimination from those for whom ethnic identity was

made more salient. Third, to tie our study to the existing literature that focuses on prosocial

behavior exhibited through economic games, our experiment examines the relevant and familiar

activity of charitable giving, but does so in the context of contributing to a real hospital that is well-

known to our subjects. We embed the experiment in Afghanistan, a weak state that struggles to

provide public goods, since we care most about understanding how private citizens respond to

solicitations to contribute to public goods provision in similar contexts.

Experimental Design

Our experiment takes place in Afghanistan, a country where ethnic identity has long featured

prominently in politics. Among ethnic groups defined by descent-based attributes (Chandra 2006),

Pashtuns are the largest, making up some 40% of the population (Barfield 2010). Though they are

split into different tribes, Pashtuns “have a powerful feeling of ethnic identity, based on a tradition

of common descent; a characteristic Indo-Iranian language, Pashto; and a communal code known

as Pashtunwali” (Riphenburg 2005, 37). Tajiks are the second largest ethnic group in the country

and speak Dari, instead of Pashto. Other non-Pashtun minority ethnic groups, most of whom

5 Specifically, “the more we are brought into physical proximity with people of another race or

ethnic background, the more we stick ‘to our own’ and the less we trust the ‘other’” (Putnam 2007,

142).


<!-- Page 9 -->


8

speak Dari, include Hazaras, Uzbeks, and Nuristani, among others, each of which has a strong

ethnic identity.

6

The modern Afghan state was founded by a Pashtun, Abdur Rahman Khan, in the 1880s

through repression and subjugation of non-Pashtun minorities. Indeed, according to one scholar,

the “sociology of Pashtun dominance over the other ethnic communities in the country forms the

very substance of political developments and state building in Afghanistan” (Shahrani 1986, 25;

quoted in Simonsen 2004, 710). With the exception of a brief period in 1929, Pashtuns controlled

the Afghan state and dominated Afghan politics until the civil war in 1992 (Barfield 2010), and

state “policies favoring Pashtuns…caused resentment among other ethnic groups” (Simonsen 2004,

709). The relationship between Pashtuns and non-Pashtuns turned even more hostile during the

civil war as the minorities challenged the Pashtuns’ claim to power and ethnic-based militias

struggled to capture the state. Over three years, at least 25,000 civilians were killed (Barfield 2010,

Lacina and Gleditsch 2005). Almost all factions engaged in arbitrary killing, torture, and sexual

violence against civilian members of other ethnic groups (Oxfam 2009), and although the Pashtun-

dominated Taliban promised to bring peace to the country, they used brute force against non-

Pashtuns, massacring Hazaras and expelling Tajiks from their villages in the northern plains of

Kabul (Barfield 2010, HRW 1998, Nordland 2012, Oxfam 2009).

6 Our focus on ethnicity is not to say that other bases of social identity in Afghanistan do not

matter, but Afghan society has long been divided mainly along language: the Pashto-speaking

dominant group vs. Dari-speaking ethnic minorities. Furthermore, recent experimental evidence

suggests that the emphasis that journalists and scholars tend to place on the political importance of

non-ethnic identities – qawm as ‘solidarity group’ being most prominent among them – may be

empirically unfounded (Jochem, Murtazashvili, and Murtazashvili 2015).


<!-- Page 10 -->


9

The post-Taliban political system has tried to promote national unity and bridge ethnic

divisions. The 2004 Constitution recognizes all ethnic identities, renders all ethnic groups equal

before the law, and even obliges the state to promote material equality through balanced

development of all areas of the country. Formal recruitment quotas for ethnic groups were

considered in the formation of the Afghanistan National Army and Afghanistan National Police

(Giustozzi and Isaqzadeh 2012).

There is some evidence that not only ethnic relations have improved since 2001, they may be

less politically divisive. At the time of our experiment, the country was in the midst of a presidential

election, deciding between an ethnic Pashtun (Ghani) and a Tajik-Pashtun mixed candidate

(Abdullah), who most considered Tajik. But issues that dominated the political landscape in the

lead up to the 2014 election – such as persistent violence and corruption – crossed ethnic lines. A

pre-election survey of over 2,000 people across multiple provinces revealed peace and security to

be the issue most respondents wanted parliament to prioritize (Callen and Long 2015). On the eve

of the election, one young man remarked, “[h]istorically, the Pashtun people have ruled this

country. But in spite of this, I don’t care who wins the election. Just put an end to the violence”

(Craig 2014).

Another poll taken just prior to the election found that an astounding 83% of

respondents would find it easy or somewhat easy to accept a non-coethnic as president (ACSOR

2014).

Our experiment takes place in Kabul, so it is worth noting that these changing attitudes may be

particularly apparent in the capital. It is an ethnically diverse city, due to increasing urban

migration, and in this way is different from the more ethnically homogeneous rural areas of the

country. Kabul’s neighborhoods tend to be ethnically segregated, though not homogeneous. In

terms of ethnic mixing in the workplace, most residents of these areas intermingle with other


<!-- Page 11 -->


10

ethnic groups since they are very likely to work outside these neighborhoods, particularly in the

city center, where you can find people representing all ethnic groups.

Within this context, we conducted our field experiment in Kabul in June 2014. Given the

historical rivalry between Pashtuns and non-Pashtun ethnic minorities, our primary interest is the

willingness of non-Pashtun minorities to aid Pashtuns. Since the ethno-linguistic divide is quite

stark, this experiment will focus on comparing the contribution of Dari-speakers to public goods

that would mainly benefit other Dari-speakers, with contributions to public goods that would

benefit Pashto-speakers.

7

Our partner organization for the experiment is EMERGENCY Hospital, a well-known

international nonprofit that provides medical care to Afghans (Mogelson 2012). Two of

Emergency’s main hospitals in Afghanistan are located in two different provinces, each dominated

by a particular ethnic group. The first is located in Anabah, in the Panjshir Valley of northern

Afghanistan, a region heavily populated by Dari-speaking minority ethnic groups. The second

hospital is located in Lashkar-gah, Helmand, in southern Afghanistan, a region dominated by

Pashtuns stated Dari as their first language. 40% of Pashtuns speak Dari as a second language and

about 37% of non-Pashtuns speak Pashto. Despite this bilingualism, the ethno-linguistic divide is

quite clean:  only 2 out of 46 subjects who stated their ethnicity as Pashtuns requested to be

enumerated in Dari and 4 out of our 213 non Pashtun subjects requested to be enumerated in

Pashto.  This indicates subjects are more comfortable speaking the language associated with their

ethnicity.


<!-- Page 12 -->


11

Pashtuns.

8 By alternating the beneficiary of the contribution between these two hospitals that are

run by the same nonprofit, we vary the ethnic identity of those who would benefit from the public

good while holding constant the attributes of the public good itself (e.g., type of services,

reputation, etc.).

Each morning over several days, we recruited male day-laborers waiting to be hired for the day

in market areas around the city.

9 This is important as subjects are drawn from the very population

about which we wish to make inferences: typical Afghan men in that they earn a low income, are

sporadically employed in a low-skill occupation, and mirror the ethnic diversity of the country.

However, while we note below how the demographic characteristics of our sample (e.g., income

and education) are in line with available data from national surveys, our results are still based on a

convenience sample, as we have no way to ensure that our subjects are representative of the

broader Afghan population.

8 These regions are highly ethnically homogeneous (http://www.icr.ethz.ch/data/geoepr). Each

ethnic group’s demographic dominance in the two provinces is key because it allows us to be

confident in assuming that our subjects infer that contributions to the Helmand hospital will

generally benefit Pashtuns and contributions to the Panjshir hospital will generally benefit non-

Pashtuns.

9 We recruited men only for two reasons. First, due to cultural norms surrounding male-female

interaction, we would have had to conduct a separate experiment for women only, and resources

and time did not permit this. Second, and more substantively, we are more interested in male

behavior with regard to out-group discrimination, as others have found discrimination effects to be

driven almost entirely by men (Fershtman and Gneezy 2001).


<!-- Page 13 -->


12

We chose different market locations each morning to avoid duplicate recruitment and to

maximize the geographic breadth of our sample. Due to the security situation in the country, it was

imperative that the experiment was completed in as few days as possible. Subjects in the same

treatment were therefore all recruited on the same day. This strategy may have affected balance of

demographics across treatment conditions, which we will control for in our regressions. While the

ideal would have been to take the day’s recruits and place them randomly into one of our three

different treatment conditions upon arrival at our enumeration location, we could not do so for

logistical reasons. Most important, we would have needed two separate and identical waiting areas

for our subjects at the enumeration location, an ethnically mixed one (for Dari-speakers in Out-

group-Real) and an ethnically homogeneous one (for Dari-speakers in In-group and Out-group-

Abstract), so as to retain the integrity of the treatments, and we could not do this at our location.

Our personnel approached potential subjects in the market area and asked if they would

participate in a survey about the labor force in Kabul. In exchange, they would be paid 500 AFN

(about $8.60 at the time, a little over a day’s wage). Subjects who provided oral consent were

transported to the enumeration location where they waited in the courtyard to be enumerated.

Enumeration of the first group of subjects began around 7 AM and the last group of subjects had

finished and exited the location by about noon, a span of about 5 hours. As illiteracy is high in

Afghanistan, we paired each subject with an enumerator to orally administer the survey and record

subjects’ answers. Subjects were called in from the courtyard in groups of 5-7 to be enumerated.

We did not force or direct interaction among waiting subjects in any of the treatment

conditions (and hence in spite of physical proximity, social interaction could be positive, negative,

both, or non-existent). Our goal was to allow participants in our study to interact as they saw fit

(Enos 2014), thus approximating the way ethnic mixing occurs in everyday life in Kabul. Crucially,


<!-- Page 14 -->


13

subjects were aware of the ethnic identity of those around them both before and during the

interview through two features of the experiment. We estimate that the walled courtyard in which

subjects waited to be enumerated is roughly 1000 square meters, small enough to enable subjects

to hear the language spoken by others waiting around them, but large enough that subjects had

choice in who to sit next to and interact with while they waited. Also, as subjects were called in

from the courtyard to be enumerated, interviewers confirmed the language used for enumeration

with his subject pairing out loud, so subjects are aware of the linguistic mix in the groups.

To maintain privacy, each subject-enumerator pair sat behind a privacy partition. Once all

subjects in the session had finished the survey, each received payment in an envelope (six 50 AFN

bills, five 20 AFN bills, and ten 10 AFN bills). Then, a solicitor told subjects that they had the

(unexpected) opportunity to contribute to a nonprofit hospital, Emergency, by reading the text

below:

10

Before you leave the room, please drop the envelope in the box by the door.

We run three treatments: In-group, Out-group-Abstract, and Out-group-Real. Recall that we

are focusing on the behavior of the Dari-speakers; hence the beneficiary hospital in the In-group

treatment is in a Dari-speaking province (Panjshir), while in both the Out-group treatments it is in

the Pashto-speaking province (Helmand). In the In-group and Out-group-Abstract treatments, we

recruited only Dari-speakers, so subjects were waiting only with other Dari-speakers before making

their contribution. This is not the case in the Out-group-Real treatment, where we recruited

Pashto-speakers alongside Dari-speakers at a ratio of 1:2 and had both groups wait in the same

courtyard for the experiment. The linguistic mix of around 1 Pashto speaker to 2 Dari speakers is

also maintained in each of the 5-7 person enumeration groups. It is important to note that because

the solicitor for the charitable contributions is the same person in all of the sessions, any effects

that we observe are due to the experimental treatments.

An important aspect of the design is that the order in which subjects were called is randomly

determined. We populated the sessions by selecting the nth person from the day’s registration list

of recruits, where n differed each day. Authors checked in with field personnel every few rounds to

Empirical Results

As our focus is on the willingness of non-Pashtun ethnic minorities (Dari-speakers) to contribute to

the dominant Pashtun ethnic group, we drop the (few) Pashtun subjects that we have from the

analysis and refer to non-Pashtun subjects simply as subjects.

13 Summary statistics of key variables

for our subjects are presented in Table 1 (Panel A). The average age of our subjects is 33. Only

half are educated at all, and those who have been average 6.8 years of education, which is in line

with the best available demographic survey evidence on the average level of education across the

entire population (Hopkins 2014). 42.5% of subjects speak more than one language; the average

number of languages spoken is 1.6, with Pashto being the most common second language. Subjects

earn about 4346 AFN ($75) per month, about average for the broader population (Hopkins 2014),

which provides them with $2.50 a day for their family. They have worked as day-laborers for about

10.4 years, on average, but most are able to find work only 2.6 days out of a week. These

individual-level attributes allow us in our regression analysis to control for factors that might

influence contributory behavior.

across the sessions, we note that there is evidence of some imbalance across treatment conditions

on several characteristics. Subjects in Out-group-Abstract worked fewer days and earn less than

Average contribution in In-Group is 20 AFN while contribution in Out-group is 21.4 AFN

when Pashtuns are not physically present (Abstract) and 16 AFN when Pashtuns are present

(Real). Figure 1 shows the kernel density plots of contributions in the three treatment conditions.

The figure indicates that the contributions in In-group and Out-group-Abstract are similar, but the

density of contributions in Out-group-Real appears quite different, particularly in how many more

subjects are giving nothing relative to the other conditions. The figure also clearly shows the non-

normality of the variables’ distributions, with outliers visible in the upper tails of the data in Out-

group-Abstract and Out-group-Real. Indeed, Shapiro-Wilk tests reject the null hypothesis that the

contributions variable is normally distributed in any of the three treatment conditions (p<0.01),

indicating the need to account for this in tests for treatment effects.

We therefore use Wilcoxon rank-sum (non-parametric) tests to test for differences in

contribution levels across treatment conditions. The results confirm that while abstract exposure

has no effect on giving relative to the in-group condition, physical exposure does. Specifically, these

tests cannot reject the null hypothesis that contributions in In-group are the same as those in Out-

group-Abstract (p=0.96), but do reject the null for contributions in In-group vs. Out-group-Real

This result is noteworthy not only for what it reveals about how prolonged exposure to the out-

group affects behavior within this experiment, but it is worth remarking on how it may fit into an

emerging set of experimental findings on the effect of time spent with the out-group. One can think

of this experiment as showing the effects of initial exposure to the out-group (including those who

might normally self-select into interaction with the out-group in everyday life and those who would

not), lasting up to about 5 hours. This length of exposure negatively affects prosocial behavior

toward the out-group. But from this experiment alone, we do not know what would happen if, say,

we lengthened that time of interaction, or if we exposed non-Pashtuns to the Pashtun out-group

repeatedly over multiple days, or if we institutionalized interaction in a more formal way.

Fortunately, others’ experimental results provide some idea of what might happen under

these conditions, and taken together, these results fill out our understanding of exposure’s effects

more generally. Enos (2014) exposes whites to Spanish-speakers for a period of minutes on a daily

basis while waiting for their commuter train, either for three days or ten days in succession. He

finds that this exposure negatively affects whites’ views of the out-group (as measured through

Alexander and Christia (2011) dovetail with this observation about the effects of repeated exposure

over a long period of time. They show that only Bosnian students who previously had been

(randomly) placed in an ethnically segregated school decreased their contributions in a public

goods game in response to increasing ethno-religious diversity of experimental sessions; students

who were attending an ethnically mixed school were not affected by the ethnic diversity of the

session. That investigation is based on a much longer period of subjects’ exposure to the out-

group, suggesting a further decrease in negative affect toward the out-group with repeated exposure

over multiple weeks, consistent with the contact hypothesis. Taken together, these three sets of

results suggest the possibility of an inverted-U-shaped curve, with discrimination toward the out-

group increasing in initial physical exposure to the out-group, but then gradually decreasing after

some peak.

Exploring the Mechanism

The fact that we observe discrimination in the Out-group-Real condition but not in Out-group-

Abstract, and that this discrimination increases with length of exposure to the out-group, is

consistent with the argument that behavior toward the out-group differs markedly depending on

the salience of ethnicity. In this section we lay out and test a further observable implication of this

mechanism, though we caution that our reasoning and analysis is post hoc and should be

considered speculative. Nevertheless, the argument is supported by the data, and the evidence is

consistent with other studies of similar behavior in countries with a history of interethnic conflict.


<!-- Page 22 -->


21

We end the section by ruling out several alternatives to the argument that would challenge our

interpretation of the main results.

We begin an investigation of the mechanism driving the observed behavior by noting that

“[f]actors that curb contact’s ability to reduce prejudice are now the most problematic theoretically,

yet the least understood”, and “the effects of these factors are likely to be moderated by the degree

to which group membership is salient during contact” (Pettigrew and Tropp 2006, 767). Indeed,

evidence from other experiments shows that subjects’ reaction to cueing the out-group is

moderated by characteristics of both the individual and the setting (Glaeser, Laibson, and

Scheinkman 2000, Haile, Sadrieh, and Verbon 2008), which informs our examination of subject

characteristics in our sample.

The political context of Afghanistan discussed above suggests two demographic factors in

particular that we might expect to moderate any effects of Dari-speaking minorities’ exposure to

the Pashto-speaking dominant group on contributions to the public good. The first is age.

Anecdotal evidence points to the youth of Afghanistan being less tied to ethnic identity than older

Afghans, perhaps because of faint to no memory of the brutal ethnic rivalries of the 1990s.

17 This is

supported by evidence on interethnic altruism from other contexts that have a similar history of

interethnic violent conflict. For example, in dictator games designed to measure interethnic

altruism and carried out in Syria, Boznia-Herzegovina, and Kosovo, Whitt, Wilson, and Mironova

(2016) find that the more time that has passed since civil conflict, the more altruistic are their

subjects toward the out-group.

17 A Kabul University professor observes that “the young Tajiks, the young Uzbeks, the young

Pashtuns, they are all friends. The ethnic card doesn’t work anymore” (Craig 2014).

The second factor is language. One of the prerequisites for quality interaction between groups

would be the ability to speak to each other. Those subjects who also can speak Pashto are better

able to interact with the out-group, possibly facilitating more positive attitudes and less

discrimination. Bilingualism here may also be a signal of selection for Dari-speaking subjects who

have interacted significantly with Pashtuns in the past.

If physical exposure increases the salience of ethnic identity, then we would expect that in Out-

group-Real, those most likely to hold out-group prejudices – the old and those who do not speak

Pashto – should decrease their contributions to the Pashtun out-group. By contrast, the young and

bilingual – who are less likely to hold such prejudice – should not be as affected by physical

exposure. We do not have an a priori theoretical rationale for predicting which of these factors –

age or language – should mediate the effect of our treatments to a greater degree.

We therefore look for age and linguistic affinity as mediating variables through regression

analysis in which the treatment variables (Out-group-Abstract and Out-group-Real) are interacted

with dummy variables indicating an age under the median of 30 (Young) and an ability to speak

Pashto (Speaks Pashto). Results of these models (which include the full set of demographic

controls) are reported in Table 3 and discussed below. In columns 2-4, we investigate the

mediating effect of language by including interactions of the treatment dummy with Speak Pashto.

Following our findings that discrimination emerges over time (see Table 2, columns 3-4), in

columns 3-4 we split the sample to Early and Late. In columns 5-7, we follow the same strategy

with Young.

Result 5: Those who do not speak the out-group’s language or are old enough to have experienced past conflicts with the out-group discriminate when the out-group is physically present. Minorities who do not speak Pashto give 13.11 (p<0.05) less in Out-group-Real than they do in the In-group treatment; older minorities give 9.42 (p<0.05) less.

In concluding our discussion of these results as indicative of out-group discrimination, we

address several possible alternative explanations and their observable implications in light of the

data. The first is that any treatment effects can be explained by the expectation of (monetary)

reciprocal generosity, as is the case in some other experiments that use trust games. Our design,

however, precludes any personal monetary return to our subjects’ contributions, and hence

behavior can only be altruistic, not strategic. The second explanation we can rule out is reputation

or social sanctioning. The complete anonymity attached to the contribution decision eliminates

sanctioning (either within the experiment or after it concluded) as explanations for behavior. The

third possibility is that observed behavior is simply an artifact of opportunity cost. While other

studies report decreased contributions in later rounds of experiments for subjects who play

iteratively, the exogenous time of exposure to the out-group allows us to isolate the part of time’s

effect on contributions that derives simply from opportunity cost of waiting from the part of the

effect that is due to physical exposure to the out-group (Out-group-Real). The difference across

conditions over time is consistent with discrimination emerging from increasing salience of

ethnicity. The fourth alternative explanation is that Dari-speakers might assume that Pashtuns will


<!-- Page 27 -->


26

“take care of their own” in the Out-group-Real condition, prompting Dari-speakers to reduce their

contributions without fear that the Pashtun-area hospital would receive less funding. But note that

if such anticipation were guiding Dari-speakers’ behavior (and not discrimination), we would

expect that not only would Dari-speakers’ contributions to the Pashtun-area hospital drop in Late

sessions in the Out-group-Real condition, but contributions also would drop noticeably in Early

sessions of that condition. In other words, wait time should not affect behavior by the logic of this

alternate explanation, but we see clearly that it does.

Conclusion

In areas where the government is either unwilling or unable to provide public goods, citizens turn

to social networks of their own in an effort to fill the gap (Humphreys and Weinstein 2009). The

question of how ethnic diversity affects willingness to contribute to such efforts is thus particularly

important in these settings. In a lab-in-the-field experiment conducted in the ethnically diverse city

of Kabul, Afghanistan, we examine how both abstract and real exposure to a dominant, Pashto-

speaking ethnic out-group affects Dari-speaking ethnic minorities’ willingness to sacrificially

contribute to enhance the welfare of strangers from that out-group, without any expectation of a

return on that investment. The fact that our subjects are drawn directly from the population whose

behavior we care about, and the fact that contribution decisions are made in the context of a real

and relevant public good, enables a more meaningful interpretation of the empirical results.

These results reveal the complicated nature of ethnic diversity’s effects on cooperative and

altruistic behavior. While subjects were just as willing to contribute to help their own in-group as

the out-group Pashtuns in the abstract, physical exposure to the out-group showed the limits of this

generosity, as contributions decreased markedly. The difference across these two ‘cues’ of the out-


<!-- Page 28 -->


27

group is evidence of discrimination, an argument supported by the fact that the longer subjects

were exposed to the out-group, the less they contributed. While the unequal status of Pashtuns and

non-Pashtuns in Afghanistan makes it difficult to generalize to contexts in which groups are more

equally situated politically and culturally, Afghanistan is far from an outlier case.  Many weak

countries transitioning out of conflict feature politically and socially unequal ethnic groups.

We reason that physical exposure to the out-group increases the salience of ethnic differences,

but found that this has non-uniform effects on prosocial behavior depending on age and ability to

speak the language of the out-group, which we speculate are measures of one’s affinity toward the

out-group. In the Afghan context, young, bilingual Afghans show evidence of having moved

beyond ethnicity as a reason to discriminate against others. These findings are in line with classic

theories which posit that assimilation to the dominant group in society occurs by gaining access to

that group’s social structures (Gordon 1964), and language and youth should help accomplish this.

In contrast, those in society least able to bridge the ethnic divide – the older and those who do not

speak Pashto – are likely to inhibit progress in this area.

Appendix Figure A4. Average Contributions of Pashtuns to Pashtun-area hospital (by waiting time in Out-group-Real)

Subgroups are ordered as follows: young Pashtuns that can also speak Dari, older Pashtuns that can also speak Dari, young Pashtuns that cannot speak Dari, older Pashtuns that cannot speak Dari. Note: contributions of Younger Pashtun who is also a Dari Speaker is 0 AFN in the Late sessions. CI bands are not included because the number of observation represented in each bar is very small (N=33 for all Pashtuns in Out-group-Real). Consistent with Figure A3, the left-most group of bars in Figure A4 is much lower than the rightmost group of bars. Also, consistent with Result 6, the length of exposure to the out-group (Darispeakers) does not affect contributions of groups in the far left or far right of the figure. Rather, it affects the middle group (Older Pashtuns who speak Dari, or Younger Pashtuns who do not speak Dari). As in Figure A3, we see that it is the Younger subjects who do not speak the other group’s language who are most affected. While Younger non-bilingual Dari-speakers in Figure A3 reduce their giving to the Pashtun-area hospital, the Younger non-bilingual Pashto-speakers here increase their giving to the Pashtun hospital. This is suggestive of the threat hypothesis.
